source_text: Filii Israelitidis et Aegyptii qui nomen maledixit. Historia aperta; sensus interior laborat. Mixto corde blasphemia nascitur.
orientation: Origen is introducing the story of the blasphemer in Leviticus 24, whose mixed parentage he reads as a figure of a divided soul.
pass_a_gloss: Sons of Israel and [the] Egyptian who [the] name cursed. [The] history [is] open; [the] sense inner labors. From [a] mixed heart blasphemy is born.

choices.english: Sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian
choices.why: Filii is plural, so the mixed parentage is stated as a class or group, not one individual; the genitives identify the mother and father.
rejected: The son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian

choices.why: The relative qui is plural, agreeing with Filii, and nomen is the direct object of maledixit.
rejected: the one who cursed the name

choices.why: Aperta is predicate adjective; Origen contrasts the plain literal account with the hidden spiritual meaning.
Laborat keeps the sense of effort or difficulty in drawing out the spiritual meaning, matching Origen's exegetical language.
Ablative of source or origin; the mixed heart is the origin of blasphemy, preserving the causal force.
Nascitur is present passive, and the metaphor of birth fits Origen's moral reading of the mixed parentage.

pass_b_english: The sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian, who cursed the name. The history is open; the inner sense labors. From a mixed heart blasphemy is born.

problems.quote: Sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian
problems.why: Latin says 'son' singular, not 'sons' plural; subject is one person.
problems.fix: The son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian
problems.ruling: 'Filii' is singular 'son' (filius); the story concerns one blasphemer, not multiple sons.

fixed: Changed 'Sons' to 'The son' because the Latin 'Filii' is singular genitive ('of the son'), not plural nominative; the subject is one person, the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian.

last_rejected.quote: The sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian
last_rejected.why: Latin says 'sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian' (two children, one from each parent), not 'sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian' as if both parents produced multiple sons together.
last_rejected.fix: The son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'Israelitidis' is feminine, 'Aegyptii' masculine; 'sons of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian' correctly renders the mixed parentage.

last_rejected.why: Subject is singular 'qui' (he who), referring to one person; 'who cursed' obscures that only one individual blasphemed.
last_rejected.ruling: 'qui nomen maledixit' is singular; 'who cursed the name' naturally reads as singular subject, no meaning lost or obscured.
